newsitem.title: UK: UK b/socs net new approvals 2.206 bln stg in June.
newsitem.headline: UK b/socs net new approvals 2.206 bln stg in June.

text.p: The British Building Societies
Association (BSA) released the following seasonally adjusted
data on lending:
(in million stg) June May June 1996
NET NEW APPROVALS 2,206 3,203 3,447
Gross advances 2,121 3,109 3,245
Socs' retail receipts(n/adj) 9,431 12,446 11,797
Retail withdrawals (n/adj) 7,587 11,568 11,945
Net receipts (n/adj) 1,844 878 -148
MORTGAGE ADVANCES AND NEW APPROVALS TO LEND (in 1000s)
Mortgage advances n/a 46,000 46,000
Approvals n/a 46,000 48,000
NOTES - approval = borrower accepts offer of advance; advance = actual loan, on average some 10 wks after commitment; advances tend to reflect new approvals made 2 or 3 mths ago.
The figures for June exclude Halifax Plc for the first time, which is now a bank rather than a building society and, from April the Alliance & Leicester.
BSA director-general Adrian Coles said the exclusion of the Halifax makes month-on-month comparisons very difficult to make.
"Having said that, however, the figures suggest that lending by committed building societies has continued to moderately increase in June."
He noted building societies attracted their biggest inflow of funds for a decade in June.

"The last time building societies had a higher inflow was in October 1986 -- before any conversions had occurred. The amount pouring into societies is even more remarkable given that the Nationwide Building Society stopped accepting new savers on 18 June.
"This is the clearest illustration yet of both the attractive rates of interest offered by societies and the intense pressure societies are under from 'carpetbaggers'"
'Carpetbagging' is a derogatory term to describe people who open building society accounts purely in order to receive free shares if the society gives up its mutual status and becomes a bank.
Coles said recent press speculation has created an atmosphere akin to a feeding frenzy in some branches.
"The only way many societies have been able to cope is reluctantly increasing the minimum balance required to open savings accounts and debarring savers from outside narrow geographical areas."
He said this sort of disruption should not be allowed to continue.

"It is quite unacceptable that service to smaller savers and genuine long-standing customers is affected. A number of commentators including the Consumers' Association, have suggested that there is a case for a moratorium on conversion so that their impact on the economy, and the structure of the housing market, can be fully assessed," Coles said.
-- Rosemary Bennett, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
